transcript.text: Price Signals
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-01
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain how prices coordinate buyers, sellers, and resource allocation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Prices coordinate decentralized decisions by communicating scarcity and changing the incentives facing buyers and sellers. Information about waiting costs can redirect users much like a price signal. A higher price raises the cost of consuming the good and encourages substitution or conservation. A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses. A supply improvement can lower price by reducing the good’s relative scarcity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses.
The price of a product falls after a new production technology spreads.
A congested road has no toll.
A price rises while quantity sold also rises.
A shortage persists because a legal ceiling prevents price from rising.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to assume that a higher price always tells buyers and sellers to do the same thing. It discourages quantity demanded while encouraging quantity supplied, coordinating opposite responses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: USING A PRICE SIGNAL

A shortage develops at the current market price. Buyers compete for the limited units, putting upward pressure on price. As price rises, quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises, reducing the shortage. The price signal helps coordinate buyers and sellers without a central allocation decision.
CHECK YOURSELF
What response does a higher market price normally encourage from sellers?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Tax Wedges and Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-02
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A per-unit tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. The wedge reduces the quantity traded because some exchanges whose benefits formerly exceeded their costs no longer occur. Tax revenue equals the per-unit wedge multiplied by the post-tax quantity, while the lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the tax wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
Use the post-tax quantity, not the original equilibrium quantity, when measuring revenue.
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax multiplied by the quantity traded after the tax.
A tax normally reduces quantity traded and creates deadweight loss from forgone exchanges.
WATCH OUT
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax times the quantity actually traded after the tax. Use the $6 wedge and 80 units here; do not multiply by the original untaxed quantity.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TAX REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price in dollars. Demand slopes down. Supply slopes up, intersecting demand at quantity 100 and price 15. A parallel Supply + tax curve above supply intersects demand at quantity 80 and price 18. At quantity 80, original supply is at price 12. Dashed guides also mark prices 10 and 20 and quantities 65, 120 and 150.

The untaxed equilibrium is $15 at 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and quantity falls to 80. The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit, so government revenue is $6 x 80 = $480.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyers pay $18 after a tax and sellers receive $12. What is the tax per unit?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Market Failures
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-03
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Identify externalities, public goods, market power, and corrective policy logic.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Markets may fail to maximize total surplus when prices omit external costs or benefits, when market power restricts trade, or when information is incomplete. Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable, creating a free-rider problem. Evaluate social marginal benefits and costs rather than assuming private incentives capture every consequence.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost.
Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.
A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude.
Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.
A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output.
WATCH OUT

Do not confuse government provision with the economic definition of a public good. Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability. Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING AN EXTERNALITY

A factory's production imposes $8 of pollution damage per unit on nearby residents, but the factory pays only its $20 private marginal cost. Social marginal cost is $20 + $8 = $28. If buyers' marginal benefit is $24, the unit looks worthwhile privately but destroys $4 of social surplus, demonstrating an external-cost market failure.
CHECK YOURSELF
What makes an effect an externality?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-07
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a price change in another good. A large positive cross-price coefficient signals a strong substitution relationship. Complementary goods connect through opposite movements between one price and the other good's demand. Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity. Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises.
Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is -0.7.
A negative cross-price coefficient means demand moves opposite the other good’s price.
The price of Product Y falls 8 percent.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse cross price with income or own price. A negative cross-price elasticity indicates complements, so higher printer prices reduce demand for ink.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING COMPLEMENTS

The price of printers rises by 10%, and demand for ink cartridges falls by 7%. Cross-price elasticity is -7% / 10% = -0.7. The negative sign indicates that printers and ink cartridges are complements because a higher price for printers reduces demand for ink.
CHECK YOURSELF
Cross-price elasticity of ink demand with respect to printer price is -0.7. If printer price falls 5%, calculate the predicted percentage change in ink demand and state its direction.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Elasticity and Total Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Connect Elasticity and Total Revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity, and the effect of a price change depends on demand elasticity. A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue. At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Calculate total revenue as price multiplied by quantity at each relevant point.
If price and total revenue move in opposite directions, demand is elastic over that range.
If price and total revenue move in the same direction, demand is inelastic over that range.
At unit elasticity, a small price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to compute elasticity without checking the associated total-revenue change. With elastic demand, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, they move together.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ELASTICITY AND REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. A straight downward-sloping Demand line runs from price 16 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 120. Its marked points are C at quantity 30, price 12; B at quantity 60, price 8; and A at quantity 90, price 4. Dashed guides show each point on both axes.

At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30, so total revenue is $12 x 30 = $360. At point B, price is $8 and quantity is 60, so revenue is $480. Moving from C to B lowers price but raises total revenue by $120, indicating elastic demand over that segment.
CHECK YOURSELF

Cruise-cabin price falls from $3,200 to $2,880 while quantity rises from 1,500 to 1,900. Calculate midpoint elasticity and both revenue totals. Is demand elastic over this range, and does revenue rise or fall?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Applications of Elasticity
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-09
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Apply Applications of Elasticity.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Elasticity helps predict tax incidence, deadweight loss, pricing responses, and other outcomes that depend on how strongly quantity responds. Market power is stronger when buyers have fewer substitutes. Labor demand is a derived factor demand. The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden. With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden.
With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.
More responsive buyers and sellers reduce traded quantity more when a tax wedge is introduced.
A firm estimates demand elasticity at 2.1.
Elastic demand produces a larger percentage quantity response to a given percentage price change.
WATCH OUT

Distinguish who sends the tax payment from who bears its economic burden. The less responsive side has fewer ways to avoid the tax, so compare demand and supply elasticities before assigning the burden.
WORKED EXAMPLE: PREDICTING TAX INCIDENCE

Two sides of a market face a $6 tax. Buyers have few substitutes and reduce purchases only slightly, while sellers can redirect output to other markets. Demand is less elastic than supply, so buyers bear more of the tax through a larger increase in the price they pay.
CHECK YOURSELF
If supply is much less elastic than demand, sellers usually bear:?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-11
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the seller's willingness to accept. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Producer surplus is the price-cost gap across units supplied. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a seller's willingness to accept or marginal cost and the price received.
Individual producer surplus equals price received minus willingness to accept.
On a graph, producer surplus is the area above supply and below the market price up to the quantity traded.
A seller whose cost exceeds the market price does not make that trade.
WATCH OUT
Producer surplus is the price received minus willingness to accept, summed over units sold. Do not confuse this per-unit price-cost gap with total revenue.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING PRODUCER SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The supply intercept is $6, so producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is the full area above supply not producer surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-12
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total surplus equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus and measures the gains created by exchange. Each trade adds to total surplus when the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the seller's opportunity cost. Total surplus is maximized when every mutually beneficial trade occurs and no trade with a cost above its value is completed.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Add consumer surplus and producer surplus to obtain total surplus.
For each possible trade, compare the buyer's willingness to pay with the seller's opportunity cost.
A trade creates gains when buyer value exceeds seller cost.
On a graph, total surplus is the area between demand and supply up to the quantity traded.
WATCH OUT
Total surplus adds consumer and producer surplus. A payment between buyers and sellers changes its distribution; a trade whose cost exceeds buyer value reduces total surplus.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TOTAL SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
The graph's equilibrium is 8 units at $14. Consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64, and producer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32. Total surplus is therefore $64 + $32 = $96.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyer value is $17 and seller cost is $22. Efficient action?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-14
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A price or policy change can transfer surplus between buyers and sellers and can destroy surplus by preventing mutually beneficial trades. A transfer changes who receives existing gains without changing their total. Deadweight loss is different: it represents gains from exchange that disappear because quantity moves away from the efficient level.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Establish the initial consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus before the change.
Recalculate those areas after the price change or policy intervention.
Separate transfers between buyers and sellers from surplus that disappears entirely.
Deadweight loss represents mutually beneficial trades prevented by the change.
WATCH OUT
A demand curve and price are enough to calculate consumer surplus. A change in consumer surplus alone does not establish the change in producer surplus, total surplus, or deadweight loss.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING A CHANGE IN CONSUMER SURPLUS

Demand slopes from price 20 at zero quantity to zero at 20. At price 12 quantity is 8 and the consumer-surplus triangle is 32. At price 8 quantity is 12 and the larger consumer-surplus triangle is 72. Distinct hatching marks these overlapping areas. No supply curve, producer surplus or deadweight loss is claimed.

At price P1 = $12, quantity is 8 and consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($20 - $12) = $32. At P2 = $8, quantity rises to 12 and consumer surplus becomes 1/2 x 12 x ($20 - $8) = $72. The price decrease raises consumer surplus by $40. These demand-side areas do not identify a transfer or deadweight loss without supply-side information.
CHECK YOURSELF
Consumer surplus rises from $32 to $72 after a price decrease. What is the gain, and can this information alone establish the change in total surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-15
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Efficiency concerns the size of total surplus, while equity concerns how benefits and costs are distributed. The efficiency result is positive analysis; deciding whether the distribution is fair adds a normative criterion. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use total surplus to evaluate efficiency and distributional evidence to evaluate equity.
Recognize that the allocation with the largest total surplus need not be the most equal.
Remember that measured willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay.
A policy judgment requires an explicit value choice when efficiency and equity point in different directions.
WATCH OUT
Efficiency compares total gains; equity evaluates their distribution. Greater total surplus does not by itself establish that a policy is fair.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WEIGHING EFFICIENCY AND EQUITY

Policy A creates $500 of total surplus divided evenly between buyers and sellers. Policy B creates $520 of total surplus but gives $500 to sellers and $20 to buyers. Policy B is more efficient because total surplus is larger, but whether its distribution is more equitable is a separate normative judgment.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says efficiency requires equal gains. Correction?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Production & Diminishing Marginal Product
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-20
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Production & Diminishing Marginal Product.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In the short run, at least one input is fixed. Marginal product is the extra output from one more unit of a variable input. With fixed equipment, additional workers may eventually add less output than earlier workers. Diminishing marginal product means the addition falls; total product can still rise.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the fixed input and the variable input.
Marginal product is the change in total product from one more worker.
Diminishing marginal product begins when successive output additions fall.
Negative marginal product means another worker actually reduces total output.
WATCH OUT
Do not wait for marginal product to become negative. It is diminishing as soon as the next worker adds less output than the previous worker.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DIMINISHING MARGINAL PRODUCT

Total product rises from 34 units with three workers to 46 with four, so the fourth worker's marginal product is 12. The fifth worker raises output from 46 to 56, giving marginal product of 10. Output still increases, but the smaller addition shows diminishing marginal product.
CHECK YOURSELF
A sixth worker raises output from 56 to 64. Calculate that worker's marginal product. Is marginal product diminishing, and is total product still rising?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Cost Components & Cost Schedules
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-21
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Complete short-run cost schedules using total and average cost identities
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In the short run, total fixed cost (TFC) does not change with output, while total variable cost (TVC) rises or falls as production changes. Total cost combines both components: TC = TFC + TVC. For positive output Q, divide each total by Q: AFC = TFC / Q, AVC = TVC / Q, and ATC = TC / Q = AFC + AVC. At zero output, TVC is normally zero, TC equals TFC, and average costs are undefined because division by zero is impossible. On a total-cost graph, the vertical distance between TC and TVC equals TFC at every quantity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A cost-schedule row is missing TFC, TVC, or TC.
A fixed payment remains even when current output is zero.
A cost changes when labor, materials, or production changes.
The vertical gap between TC and TVC is compared across quantities.
Total costs must be converted to per-unit AFC, AVC, or ATC.
WATCH OUT

Do not subtract or multiply fixed and variable cost when finding total cost: add them. Also distinguish total fixed cost from average fixed cost. TFC stays constant as output changes, but AFC = TFC / Q falls as the same fixed amount is spread across more units. Average costs are not defined at Q = 0.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BUILDING A COST SCHEDULE

At Q = 120, TC is $1,200 and TVC is $800. TFC is the difference: $400. Divide each total by output to obtain AFC = $3.33, AVC = $6.67, and ATC = $10.00, rounded to cents. The completed row satisfies TC = TFC + TVC and ATC = AFC + AVC.
CHECK YOURSELF
At Q = 10, a schedule shows TFC = $90 and TC = $250. What are TVC, AFC, AVC, and ATC, and how can you verify that AFC + AVC = ATC?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-22
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost express costs per unit of output. Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. Average fixed cost falls as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units, while average variable cost changes with the productivity and price of variable inputs.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Divide fixed cost by output for average fixed cost and variable cost by output for average variable cost.
Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units.
Use per-unit measures only when output is positive.
WATCH OUT
Average costs are per unit; total costs are not. Subtract AVC from ATC to find AFC, then multiply AFC by positive output to recover total fixed cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING AVERAGE-COST CURVES

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: costs in dollars. Curves are labeled MC, AC and AVC. MC first dips slightly and then rises. It crosses AVC at its minimum, quantity 200 and cost 10. At quantity 400, MC crosses AC at its minimum of 20, while AVC is 12. Dashed guides mark the quantities and costs. AC remains above AVC.

At 400 units, the graph shows average cost of $20 and average variable cost of $12. Because AC = AVC + AFC, average fixed cost is $20 - $12 = $8 per unit. The gap between AC and AVC is therefore the firm's average fixed cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
At Q = 30, AVC is $14 and ATC is $24. Calculate AFC and total fixed cost. Verify your answer by multiplying the per-unit gap by output.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-23
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in output. If labor is the only variable input and its wage is fixed, divide the added worker's wage by that worker's marginal product. Lower marginal product then means higher cost per extra unit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for the change in total cost caused by producing one additional unit.
Compute marginal cost as the change in total cost divided by the change in output.
A fixed-cost change does not change marginal cost, but a variable-input cost change usually does.
When marginal product falls, marginal cost tends to rise if the input price is unchanged.
WATCH OUT
Hold the wage and other input conditions fixed when linking marginal product to marginal cost. A fixed-cost change alone does not change the cost of an extra unit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: LINKING MARGINAL PRODUCT AND COST

Each additional worker costs $120. The fourth adds 12 units, so added cost per unit is $120 / 12 = $10. The fifth adds 10 units, so it is $120 / 10 = $12. With the wage unchanged, diminishing marginal product raises marginal cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
At a wage of $120, another worker adds 8 units. What is the added labor cost per unit of output?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Cost Curves: Relationships & Shifts
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-24
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Cost Curves: Relationships & Shifts.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Short-run cost curves move differently because fixed costs affect AFC and ATC, while variable-input costs affect AVC, ATC, and MC. A below-average marginal observation pulls the average down. Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model. A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
A technology improvement reduces the variable input needed at every output.
Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model.
A firm receives a property-tax increase that does not depend on output.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to mix fixed and variable shifts. A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHIFTING SHORT-RUN COST CURVES

Quantity horizontal; cost per unit vertical. Original ATC equals AVC plus 250 divided by Q. Higher fixed cost makes ATC equal AVC plus 500 divided by Q, above original ATC at every positive output. AVC and MC remain unchanged. The ATC-AVC gap declines with Q for either fixed-cost amount.

Suppose the firm signs a more expensive lease while output and variable input prices are unchanged. The higher fixed cost raises average fixed cost and therefore shifts ATC upward. AVC and MC remain in the positions shown because neither depends on fixed cost. The production decision at the margin is unchanged.
CHECK YOURSELF
With fixed cost unchanged, why does the ATC-AVC gap shrink as output rises? How is that different from an increase in the lease payment at a fixed output?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Minimum Efficient Scale & Constant Returns to Scale
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-27
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Minimum Efficient Scale & Constant Returns to Scale.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which long-run average cost reaches its minimum. Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached. MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Find the lowest point of the long-run average-cost curve.
Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which that minimum cost is attained.
A flat minimum indicates a range of outputs with constant returns to scale.
Do not confuse a flat average-cost segment with output remaining unchanged.
WATCH OUT
Minimum efficient scale is the first output attaining minimum LRAC, not the midpoint or end of a flat minimum-cost interval.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING MINIMUM EFFICIENT SCALE

Quantity horizontal and long-run average cost vertical. LRAC falls to 12 at quantity 60, stays flat at 12 from 60 through 90, then rises. Minimum efficient scale is 60, the first output at the flat minimum. The flat interval illustrates constant returns to scale.

LRAC first reaches $12 at 60 units and remains at $12 through 90 units. Minimum efficient scale is therefore 60. The flat 60-to-90 interval illustrates constant returns to scale: output can expand proportionally without changing long-run cost per unit.
CHECK YOURSELF
If LRAC first reaches its minimum at 5,000 units and remains flat until 8,000, MES is:?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Market Structure, Price Taking & Firm Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-28
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Connect Market Structure, Price Taking & Firm Revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A perfectly competitive firm takes the market price as given, so price, average revenue, and marginal revenue are equal. Market power changes the firm's revenue conditions; the competitive firm takes price. Price taking makes each sold unit add the same amount to revenue, setting up the later MR-versus-MC output rule.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for many firms, a standardized product, easy entry, and no control over market price.
A price-taking firm can sell another unit without lowering its price.
For the competitive firm, price, average revenue, and marginal revenue are equal.
Treat market price as a horizontal line in the individual firm's graph.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to separate price, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a price-taking firm. Under perfect competition, P = AR = MR.
WORKED EXAMPLE: REVENUE FOR A PRICE TAKER

The firm takes a market price of $25. Selling 50 units yields total revenue of $25 x 50 = $1,250. Each additional unit adds $25 to revenue without lowering the price on earlier units. Thus P = AR = MR. Choosing the profit-maximizing output is a separate later step.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why does total revenue rise linearly with output?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-32
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost. The tax is tied to each unit produced. MC gives the additional cost of supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost as firm supply.
A variable-input cost increase shifts marginal cost and short-run supply upward or left.
A fixed-cost change shifts average total cost but leaves marginal cost and short-run supply unchanged.
Distinguish a movement along supply caused by price from a shift caused by production conditions.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume fixed cost shifts supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost. Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING SHORT-RUN FIRM SUPPLY

Horizontal axis: firm quantity; vertical axis: cost / revenue. Horizontal P = MR = AR is at 10, below the entire AVC curve. MC crosses minimum AVC at A, quantity 22 and cost 20. Other marked points on rising MC are B near quantity 36 and cost 30, C near quantity 44 and cost 41 at minimum ATC, and D near quantity 50 and cost 50. Unprinted coordinates are approximate. ATC is above AVC.

The firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of MC at and above minimum AVC, which begins at point A: 22 units and $20. For example, if market price rises to $30, the firm supplies the quantity at point B, about 36 units. MC below A is not part of supply because the firm shuts down.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which MC segment is competitive short-run supply?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-33
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace entry, exit, zero economic profit, normal profit, and long-run competitive adjustment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Entry and exit move a competitive industry toward long-run equilibrium with zero economic profit. More firms supply more total output at each price. At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit. Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.
Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
Long-run industry assessment 10: Demand falls in a constant-cost industry and some firms leave.
Long-run industry assessment 11: Demand rises in a constant-cost industry and entry is unrestricted.
WATCH OUT

Do not miss long run equilibrium conditions. At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit. Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY AND ZERO ECONOMIC PROFIT

Two panels. Left, Market: horizontal axis market quantity; vertical axis price. S slopes up and D slopes down, intersecting at quantity 100 and price 25. Right, Representative firm: horizontal axis firm quantity; vertical axis cost / revenue. Horizontal P = MR = AR at 25 meets MC and minimum ATC at quantity 50. At that quantity, AVC is 17, explicitly labeled and connected by dashed guides. ATC and AVC are U-shaped. Both panels share price 25.

If firms initially earn economic profit, entry expands market supply and pushes price down. If they incur losses, exit reduces supply and pushes price up. The graph shows the endpoint: P = MC, and price equals minimum ATC at $25 and 50 units. Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs, so no entry or exit pressure remains.

Monopoly Power, Barriers to Entry & Sources of Monopoly

MICRO-36
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Monopoly Power, Barriers to Entry & Sources of Monopoly.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A monopoly has durable market power because barriers prevent close rivals from entering and eroding that power. Barriers can keep profit from triggering the entry response that erodes profit in competitive markets. Natural monopoly can make one-firm production cost-efficient while still creating a market-power problem.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A city has one coffee shop today, but entry is easy and several rivals are preparing to open.
A software firm is the only seller this year.
The current one-seller market does not by itself establish durable monopoly power.
One seller becomes a durable monopoly only when entry is meaningfully blocked.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat any large firm as monopoly. Durable monopoly power depends on the relevant market and barriers to entry. A monopoly requires meaningful barriers to entry, not merely one seller at a moment in time.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING A BARRIER TO ENTRY

A city grants one firm the exclusive right to distribute water through its pipe network. Even if another firm could supply water, the exclusive license prevents legal entry. This is a legal barrier, distinct from economies of scale that can also make a single network less costly. Identifying the barrier does not by itself determine the best regulated price.

Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price

Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A monopolist compares marginal revenue with marginal cost to choose output, then reads the corresponding price from demand. In the displayed interior solution, MR exceeds MC before their crossing and falls below MC afterward. The output decision and the price decision are separate; marginal cost need not always slope upward.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Find the output where MR crosses MC from above in the interior solution.
Move vertically from that output to the demand curve to find the monopoly price.
Keep the output decision and price decision separate: marginal conditions determine quantity, demand determines price.
Do not set price equal to marginal revenue or marginal cost unless the graph happens to imply it.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to read monopoly price from the marginal-revenue curve. Find output where MR = MC, then read the price buyers will pay from demand.

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D slopes down from price 60 at quantity 0 to zero at 120. MR slopes down more steeply, reaching zero at 60. At quantity 40, MR and rising MC meet at 20; demand is at 40 and ATC at 45, with dashed guides. Demand and MC intersect near quantity 67 and price 27. ATC is U-shaped, reaching its minimum to the right of quantity 40. The 67 and 27 intersection values are approximate as labeled.

The monopolist first finds output where MR = MC, which occurs at 40 units and a marginal value of $20. It then moves up to the demand curve, where buyers will pay $40 for 40 units. The profit-maximizing choice is therefore Q = 40 and P = $40, not the $20 MR value.

Price Discrimination

MICRO-42
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Price Discrimination.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices for the same product when resale can be prevented. Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist. Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable. Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.
Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.
Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.
The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.
Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to disconnect wtp from first degree efficiency. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING PRICE DISCRIMINATION

A theater charges students $8 and other adults $14 for the same seat. The policy can persist only if students cannot resell discounted tickets to adults; otherwise arbitrage would erase the price difference. Verification separates the groups, and the different prices reflect different demand elasticities.

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown

MICRO-44
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown uses MR = MC, firm demand, ATC, and AVC to determine output, price, profit or loss, and short-run shutdown. The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use marginal revenue and rising marginal cost to choose the firm's output.
Read price and average total cost at that output to determine profit or loss.
Use average variable cost to determine whether the firm operates or shuts down in the short run.
Keep output choice, profit measurement, and shutdown analysis as three distinct steps.
WATCH OUT
Separate profit from shutdown. A fixed-cost increase can create an economic loss without changing marginal cost or the benefit of operating; compare revenue with variable cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN FIRM DECISION

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

The displayed baseline has Q = 36 and P = ATC = $27, so economic profit is zero. Consider a higher fixed lease cost of $108, with demand and variable costs unchanged. Output and price stay at that baseline, but ATC rises by $3 and the loss is $108. The firm still operates if revenue covers variable cost; loss alone does not imply shutdown.

Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In monopolistic competition, short-run profit attracts entry and short-run loss causes exit until economic profit is zero. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Short-run economic profit attracts entry, which reduces each incumbent firm's demand.
Short-run losses cause exit, which raises the demand facing surviving firms.
Long-run equilibrium occurs when the firm's demand is tangent to average total cost and economic profit is zero.
Distinguish zero economic profit from zero accounting profit.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate zero economic and accounting profit. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY, EXIT, AND LONG-RUN PROFIT

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

Short-run profit attracts competing varieties, reducing demand for each incumbent. Adjustment continues until demand is tangent to ATC at the chosen output. The graph shows that endpoint at 36 units and $27, where revenue and cost both equal $972. Tangency eliminates economic profit; it does not put output at minimum ATC.

Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition

Outcome: Analyze Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition.

THE CORE IDEA

Advertising can give buyers product information, persuade them, or build a brand. Information about prices, hours, or features can reduce search costs. Persuasive messages can change preferences or price sensitivity. Nonprice competition also includes quality, convenience, service, and variety.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged.
Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase.
A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand.
A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information.
A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive.

Do not treat every advertisement as useful information or as waste. Ask what it tells buyers and whether it changes their ability to compare products.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INFORMATIVE OR PERSUASIVE ADVERTISING?

A pharmacy advertises that a prescription costs $8 and that it stays open until 10 p.m. Buyers can compare stores more easily, so search costs fall; this is informational advertising. A separate campaign associates the brand with status without adding product facts; that campaign is persuasive advertising. Both compete without directly cutting price.

Monopolistic competition trades some cost and allocative efficiency for product variety and differentiated consumer choices. Variety may create utility even while markup and excess capacity remain. Variety can create utility even with efficiency costs. Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Variety may create utility even while markup and excess capacity remain.
Variety can create utility even with efficiency costs.
Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.
Two markets have the same total production cost.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WEIGHING THE VALUE OF VARIETY

Two bakeries offer different breads. A neighborhood values having both varieties, but dividing sales between the bakeries can leave each producing below its lowest-cost scale. More variety can therefore benefit buyers while raising cost per loaf. A welfare judgment weighs those benefits against the extra resource cost; a markup alone does not measure the value of variety.

THE CORE IDEA

A cartel coordinates firms to restrict industry output and raise price as a monopolist would. Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.
The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.
A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
Three firms agree to keep prices high.
WATCH OUT
Do not miss individual incentive to defect. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.

If Column keeps the agreement, Row gets 8 by undercutting rather than 6 by keeping it. If Column undercuts, Row gets 3 rather than 2 by undercutting. Column faces the same incentives. Both undercut and receive 3 each, although keeping the agreement would give 6 each. Individual incentives can undermine a mutually beneficial agreement.

Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence

MICRO-51
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze repeated games, credible commitments, entry deterrence, and sequential strategic choices.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

In a sequential game, one player acts before another. Work backward from the last decision: identify the action that the later player will actually prefer, then use that response to evaluate the first move. A threat is credible only if carrying it out would be worthwhile when the decision arrives. Repeated interaction can make future consequences matter, but no present-value calculation is needed here.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Determine whether firms interact once or expect to meet again.
Compare the immediate gain from cheating or entering with future losses from retaliation.
A threat affects behavior only when carrying it out would be credible.
Longer relationships, patience, and observable actions make cooperative outcomes easier to sustain.
WATCH OUT
A threatened response is not automatically credible. Compare the later player's payoffs at the decision point before using the threat to predict the first move.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING A CREDIBLE THREAT

Sequential game tree; payoffs are ordered Entrant, Incumbent. The Entrant moves first. Stay out ends with payoffs (0, 12). Enter leads to the Incumbent decision node. From that node, Accommodate ends with (6, 7), and Fight ends with (negative 3, 3). Branch labels identify the actions; each payoff belongs to its branch endpoint.

The game tree is solved backward. If entry occurs, the incumbent receives 7 by accommodating and 3 by fighting, so accommodation is the credible response on that branch. Anticipating it, the entrant compares 6 from entering with 0 from staying out and enters. The backward-induction outcome is Enter, then Accommodate.

Factor Markets & Labor Demand

Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use marginal productivity to analyze labor demand, wages, and employment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Labor demand is derived from the value workers add to output. Marginal product of labor is the extra output from one more worker. For a price-taking seller, VMP = output price x MPL. A profit-maximizing firm hires labor up to the point where VMP equals the wage.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A wage change causes movement along labor demand; productivity or output-price changes shift labor demand.
Higher product demand, output price, or worker productivity shifts labor demand right.
Worker preferences, population, migration, training, and alternative jobs can shift labor supply.
Competitive wage and employment occur where market labor demand intersects market labor supply.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse MPL with VMP. MPL is extra physical output; VMP converts that output into dollars by multiplying by the output price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPETITIVE LABOR-MARKET EQUILIBRIUM

Horizontal axis: hundreds of warehouse workers; vertical axis: hourly wage in dollars. Labor Demand slopes down from wage 30 at quantity 0 to zero at 120 hundreds. Labor Supply slopes up from wage 10. They intersect at wage 20 and quantity 40 hundreds of workers, with dashed guides to both axes. Supply lies above demand to the right of that intersection.

Suppose output sells for $5 and the marginal worker adds 4 units per hour. VMP is $5 x 4 = $20 per hour, matching a $20 wage. The graph shows market equilibrium at that wage and 40 hundreds of workers, or 4,000 workers. A higher output price raises VMP at each employment level and shifts labor demand right.

If the output price rises while worker productivity is unchanged, what happens to labor demand?

Consumer Choice

Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use a budget constraint and preferences to identify the best affordable bundle.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A budget constraint shows affordable bundles at given income and prices. Its intercepts show the most of either good a consumer can buy. An indifference curve connects bundles the consumer ranks equally. The best affordable bundle reaches the highest available preference level; in this example, its curve just touches the budget line.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Bundles inside or on the budget line are feasible; bundles outside it are infeasible.
An income change shifts the line in parallel when prices are fixed.
A change in one price pivots the line around the unchanged intercept.
Compare the highest preference curve that can be reached without exceeding the budget.

Spending the whole budget is not enough to prove optimality. The chosen bundle must also provide the highest attainable preference ranking.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BEST AFFORDABLE BUNDLE

Horizontal axis: Good X; vertical axis: Good Y. A straight budget line runs from 40 units of Y at X = 0 to 20 units of X at Y = 0. Marked bundle A is X = 10 and Y = 20. At A the budget line is tangent to solid IC2. Dashed IC1 lies below IC2 and intersects the feasible set; dashed IC3 lies above IC2 and outside the budget line. All three indifference curves slope down and are convex toward the origin.

The budget line reaches 20 units of X or 40 units of Y, so its slope is -2. Bundle A contains 10 units of X and 20 of Y. At A, the budget line is tangent to IC2, the highest attainable indifference curve. IC3 is preferred but lies outside the feasible set, while IC1 is attainable but provides a lower ranking.

Condorcet Paradox & Voting Cycles
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-66
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain how pairwise majority rule can generate cyclic collective preferences.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Even when every voter has a consistent ranking, pairwise majority voting can produce a cycle: A defeats B, B defeats C, and C defeats A. The group then has no option that defeats every alternative, and agenda order can affect the final outcome.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
There are at least three alternatives and voters rank them differently.
Compare alternatives two at a time using majority rule.
The collective relation cycles even though each individual's ranking is consistent.
Because no option is a universal majority winner, agenda order may matter.
WATCH OUT
A voting cycle does not require irrational voters. Individually transitive rankings can aggregate into an intransitive majority relation.
WORKED EXAMPLE: THREE VOTERS, THREE OPTIONS

Using the rankings, A defeats B by 2 votes to 1; B defeats C by 2 to 1; and C defeats A by 2 to 1. Each voter has a consistent ranking, yet the group cycles. With no option beating every rival, the order of pairwise votes can affect the final survivor.

Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-67
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain the basic limitation on combining individual rankings into a social ranking.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

With at least three alternatives, Arrow's theorem shows that no ranked-choice social decision rule can guarantee all of a specified set of desirable conditions at once. The result identifies a tradeoff among aggregation properties; it does not prove that democracy or every voting system is impossible.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The problem combines individual rankings into a complete and consistent social ranking.
Desirable conditions include respecting unanimity and avoiding control by one dictator.
Independence of irrelevant alternatives limits how an outside option may change a pairwise ranking.
The theorem concerns simultaneous guarantees under its conditions, not whether voting can occur.
WATCH OUT
Do not conclude that no voting system works or that democracy is impossible. The theorem applies to ranked aggregation and the simultaneous satisfaction of specified conditions.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DESIRABLE RULES IN TENSION

A community wants all five guarantees in the table. With at least three alternatives, Arrow's theorem says no rule combining unrestricted individual rankings can always provide every guarantee. The introductory lesson is a design tradeoff among reasonable goals, not that elections cannot produce winners.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which is accurate: Arrow identifies incompatible guarantees under stated conditions, or proves that no election can produce a winner?

Median Voter Theorem
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-68
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain why majority-rule competition can favor the median voter's position under specific assumptions.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

When policy lies on one dimension, preferences are single-peaked, and decisions use majority rule, the median voter's preferred position has a special advantage. Policies or candidates may move toward it because alternatives on either side can be defeated by a majority.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Place voters along one policy dimension and identify the middle preferred position.
Each voter has a single peak and prefers positions less as they move away from it.
Pairwise decisions use majority rule.
Competition can favor the median, but the conclusion depends on these assumptions.
WATCH OUT
The median voter does not always decide elections. Multidimensional policy, non-single-peaked preferences, turnout, institutions, or other departures can break the result.
WORKED EXAMPLE: THE PIVOTAL POLICY POSITION

One policy axis marks ideal points 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. Median is 30. Voters at 10, 20 and 30 form a majority for 30 against a higher proposal. Voters at 30, 40 and 50 form a majority for 30 against a lower proposal. The example assumes single-peaked preferences and pairwise majority rule.

Five voters prefer policy levels 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50. The ordered middle preference is 30. Against a proposal below 30, the voters at 30, 40, and 50 form a majority for 30; against one above 30, the voters at 10, 20, and 30 form a majority for 30. Under one-dimensional, single-peaked preferences and majority rule, the median position can defeat alternatives on either side.
